title: Placement: find your starting point

bigIdea.text: A short test finds where you should start, so you don't repeat what you know or skip what you don't.

proper.text: The ladder has 4 levels: (1) letters; (2) letters with harakat; (3) joined words, as printed in the mushaf (the written Quran); (4) a short ayah aloud.

Harakat (singular: harakah) are the small vowel marks on letters. Fatha is a short 'a' (a small stroke above), kasra a short 'i' (a small stroke below) and damma a short 'u' (a small waw-shape above).
You start at level 1. Pass a level and you climb to the next. Two fails at the same level stop the test, and you start learning at that level.
Level 4: listen to Sheikh al-Minshawi recite a short ayah, recite it back, then rate your attempt honestly against his.
Placement is not a grade. Starting a little low costs a few minutes; starting too high leaves gaps that cost far more later.

memoryHook.text: Climb until you slip twice: that step is where you start.

extras.text: Level 2 can also show sukun (no vowel), shadda (the letter is doubled) and tanwin (an added 'n': -an, -in, -un).

note.text: The short ayah used in this lesson's listen and echo steps.

questions.q: When does the placement ladder stop?
options: After two fails at the same level
After your first mistake anywhere
Only after all 4 levels, whatever happens
After exactly 10 minutes
explain: Right: two fails at one level show that this is your starting point.
One slip is allowed; a second fail at the same level stops it.
It stops early when a level is clearly too hard, to save you time.
It is not timed; it follows your answers.

options: Letters with harakat (vowel marks)
Single letters with no marks
A short ayah aloud
Your voice range
explain: Right.
That is level 1.
That is level 4.
Your voice range was measured during setup, not in placement.

questions.q: At level 4, how is your short ayah judged in this placement?
options: You listen to Sheikh al-Minshawi, recite it, then rate your attempt against his
A teacher online marks it
It is not judged at all
The app only checks how loud you were
explain: Right: an honest self-rating against the reference voice.
Nothing is sent to anyone; your recordings stay on your phone.
It is judged, by you, against Sheikh al-Minshawi.
Loudness says nothing about correct reading.

options: Small marks on letters that show the short vowels
The dots that tell letters apart
The numbers at the end of each ayah
Signs that show where you may pause
explain: Right: fatha, kasra and damma are the main three.
The dots are part of the letters themselves.
Those are ayah numbers.
Those are pause (waqf) signs.

questions.q: A small slanted stroke ABOVE a letter is…
options: fatha: a short 'a'
kasra: a short 'i'
damma: a short 'u'
tanwin: an added 'n'
explain: Right.
Kasra is the stroke BELOW the letter.
Damma looks like a small waw above the letter.
Tanwin is a doubled vowel mark, not a single stroke.

options: Kasra: a small stroke below the letter
Fatha: a small stroke above the letter
Damma: a small waw-shape above the letter
Shadda: a small w-shape above the letter
explain: Right.
Fatha gives 'a'.
Damma gives 'u'.
Shadda doubles the letter; it is not a vowel.

options: Reading letters joined into whole words, as printed in the mushaf
Reciting two ayat in one breath
Reciting at the same time as Sheikh al-Minshawi
Writing words by hand
explain: Right: the mushaf is the written Quran.
Breath planning comes in Stage 3.
That is a different practice mode, not this level.
The app checks reading, not handwriting.

questions.q: In the echo drill, what do you do?
options: Listen to Sheikh al-Minshawi recite a phrase, then recite it back
Recite first, then listen to him
Recite at exactly the same time as him
Read silently without recording
explain: Right: he calls, you answer.
In echo he goes first, so you copy a fresh model.
Reciting together is a different practice mode.
Echo records your answer so you can compare.

questions.q: Where does the placement test start?
options: At level 1, letters
At level 4, the short ayah
At whichever level you pick
At Stage 2, tajweed
explain: Right: everyone starts at the bottom and climbs.
You reach the ayah only after passing the first three levels.
The ladder decides, so the result is fair.
Placement covers reading, which comes before tajweed.

questions.q: You fail level 2 twice. What happens?
options: The test stops, and you start learning at letters with harakat
You move on to level 3 anyway
You go back to the start of level 1
You are locked out of the app
explain: Right: that level is your starting point.
Two fails at a level stop the climb.
You keep what you passed; level 1 is already done.
Placement only chooses where you start.

questions.q: You slip once at level 3, then read the next items well. What happens?
options: You carry on: only a second fail at the same level stops the test
The test stops at once
You drop back to level 1
Level 3 is skipped
explain: Right: one slip is allowed.
One slip is not enough to stop it.
A slip does not send you back.
Each level is checked in turn.

questions.q: In what order does the ladder climb?
options: Letters → letters with harakat → joined words → short ayah
Short ayah → joined words → letters with harakat → letters
Letters → joined words → letters with harakat → short ayah
Letters with harakat → letters → short ayah → joined words
explain: Right: each step builds on the one before.
That is upside down: the ayah is the top step.
Harakat come before joined words.
Plain letters come first.

questions.q: Why should you rate your level-4 recitation honestly?
options: A start that is too high leaves gaps; an honest rating puts you where lessons help most
Low ratings are punished
A high rating unlocks the maqam lessons early
Your rating is shared with other learners
explain: Right: placement is not a grade.
Nothing is punished; the rating only chooses where you start.
Maqamat come after correct reading and tajweed.
Ratings and recordings stay on your phone.

questions.q: When you compare your ayah with Sheikh al-Minshawi's, what comes first?
options: Correct letters and vowels, then melody
Melody, then the letters
Speed: match his tempo exactly
Loudness: match his volume
explain: Right: beauty never comes before correct reading.
A beautiful tune with wrong letters is still wrong.
Speed matters least at this stage.
Volume is not part of correct reading.

questions.q: A shadda (a small w-shape above a letter) means…
options: The letter is doubled: said once without a vowel, then again with its vowel
The letter is silent
The vowel is long
The letter is heavy
explain: Right.
Shadda makes a letter stronger, not silent.
Long vowels come from the letters alif, waw and ya, not from shadda.
Heaviness belongs to certain letters, not to the shadda.

questions.q: Tanwin (a doubled vowel mark) at the end of a word adds…
options: An 'n' sound after the vowel: -an, -in or -un
A long vowel
A stop with no vowel
A heavy sound
explain: Right.
Long vowels come from the letters alif, waw and ya.
No vowel is shown by sukun.
Tanwin does not make a letter heavy.

options: Where you begin learning; it is not a grade
Whether you may use the app
Your final mark for the course
Which reciter you hear
explain: Right.
Everyone can use the whole app.
There is no final mark; mastery is per lesson.
Sheikh al-Minshawi is always the reference voice.

remnote: Placement ladder levels == 1 letters, 2 letters with harakat, 3 joined words, 4 a short ayah aloud
When placement stops == After two fails at the same level
Placement level 4 judging == Self-rated against Sheikh al-Minshawi's recitation
Harakat == Short-vowel marks: fatha 'a' (stroke above), kasra 'i' (stroke below), damma 'u' (small waw above)
Tanwin == An added 'n' after the vowel: -an, -in, -un
Self-rating order == Correct letters and vowels first, melody second
taskNow: Start the placement ladder at level 1 and keep going until it stops; at level 4, rate your ayah honestly against Sheikh al-Minshawi.
